name: Mebolazine (Dymethazine)

lead: Mebolazine (dimethazine) is an oral anabolic steroid once sold as a medicine (Dostalon, Roxilon) and later withdrawn. From about 2008 it reappeared in gray-market supplements marketed to bodybuilders for lean mass and a fuller physique.

It is a 17α-alkylated DHT derivative and an unusual dimer of methasterone, reportedly acting as a prodrug of methasterone, an androgen receptor agonist. No clinical trials were found; published research is limited to metabolism studies.

paras: It has appeared as an oral ingredient, sometimes unlisted, in supplement products used in bodybuilding.
The FDA has taken legal action against makers of supplements containing it, and it is classed with the hepatotoxic oral steroids. Human safety data are absent.

angle.text: Mebolazine is used for lean mass gains and a fuller physique: it is reportedly converted to methasterone, which activates androgen receptors and drives muscle protein gain. It turned up in gray-market supplements; no human studies exist.

lead: Mebolazine, also called dimethazine or dymethazine, is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid. It is a 17α-alkylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone and an unusual dimer of methasterone, two units joined by an azine group [1]. People who seek it are after the usual outcome of anabolic steroids: more lean muscle mass and a larger, harder-looking physique.

Wikipedia reports that it reportedly acts as a prodrug of methasterone and that it was once marketed as the medicines Dostalon and Roxilon but is no longer sold [1]. Since about 2008 it has been found as an unlisted ingredient in some dietary supplements, and the US FDA has taken legal action against manufacturers of such products [1]. Case reports describe it as one of the designer steroids found in a product sold as a supplement, Super DMZ Rx 2.0 [2].
No clinical trials of its effects on muscle were found. The literature consists of metabolism studies and case reports of adverse events linked to supplements that contained it.[1][2][3]
infobox: Methasterone (two units joined by an azine group)[1]
Withdrawn drug; found as undeclared supplement ingredient[1][3]

paras: Mebolazine is a synthetic steroid whose systematic name is 2α,17α-dimethyl-5α-androstan-17β-ol-3-one azine. It is a dimer of methasterone in which two steroid units are linked at the 3-position of the A-ring by an azine group, and, like many oral anabolic steroids, it is a 17α-alkylated derivative of dihydrotestosterone.[1] It is grouped with other 17α-alkylated DHT derivatives such as furazabol, oxandrolone and stanozolol, and is structurally related to bolazine.[1]

It is classified as an orally active androgen receptor agonist and is reported to act as a prodrug of methasterone, meaning the body converts it into that compound.[1] A 2016 study examined its metabolism in vitro and in vivo.[1] Wikipedia notes little further published detail on its pharmacokinetics or clinical effects.[1]

Methasterone (methyldrostanolone), the parent compound, was first described in 1956 by Syntex researchers looking for anti-tumour compounds; a 1959 paper called it a potent oral anabolic agent with weak androgenic effects, and a later reference reported about 400 percent of the anabolic and 20 percent of the androgenic activity of methyltestosterone.[4] It is hepatotoxic, with several case reports of cholestatic liver injury.[4]

Mebolazine was sold as a medicine under the names Dostalon and Roxilon but is no longer marketed and is listed as a withdrawn drug.[1] Wikipedia does not describe its original indications or development.[1]

Its modern appearance is tied to the designer steroid era. Methasterone reappeared in 2005 as the main ingredient of a supplement called Superdrol, identified in products by Don Catlin of the UCLA Olympic Laboratory and reported by the Washington Post; sellers were able to market it because the Anabolic Steroids Control Act of 1990 and its 2004 revision did not name compounds that were not commercially available when they were written. The FDA issued warnings in 2006, methasterone is now a US Schedule III substance, and WADA prohibits it.[4] Since about 2008, mebolazine itself has reportedly been added illegally to some dietary supplements, including vitamin B products, and the FDA has taken legal action against manufacturers.[1]

Muscle-building products containing hidden steroids are sold as dietary supplements and have been found by regulators and researchers: a 2015 review in Andrology described the growing presence of designer androgens in over-the-counter supplements, and Wikipedia reports a 2007 to 2016 analysis that found 776 supplements with unlisted pharmaceutical ingredients, including muscle-building products contaminated with anabolic steroids.[1][5]

A 2023 Steroids paper analysed about 16 New York residents who reported fatigue, hair loss and muscle aches between 2012 and 2013, including one hospitalised with liver damage; testing of the implicated B-50 supplements found methasterone, dimethazine and methylstenbolone, and symptoms of severe virilization were reported in a child.[3] The 2014 case report notes that methylstenbolone and dymethazine were gaining popularity among bodybuilders for their rapid effects on muscle mass and were found together in a product called Super DMZ Rx 2.0.[2]

A 2014 case report in the Journal of Investigative Medicine High Impact Case Reports described what the authors called the first case of cholestatic jaundice linked to Super DMZ Rx 2.0, a product containing methylstenbolone and dymethazine. The patient was a previously healthy 26-year-old man who took the product as directed for 30 days, and the authors noted that such supplements may hide potent androgens from consumers.[2] A 2024 review of 50 years of case reports on anabolic-androgenic steroid abuse found methylstenbolone most strongly linked to hepatic complications.[3] Wikipedia categorises mebolazine among hepatotoxins.[1] Reports in the New York cluster included hair loss, fatigue, muscle aches and liver damage.[3]

No studies found testing mebolazine as a treatment or performance aid in people. Published human data are limited to case reports of harm from supplements that contained it, and metabolism studies.[1][2][3]
